tells: Names the Sheikh as 'Sheikh Bahmanpour', embeds a short quotation then states plainly what it means ('the goal has become something other than God'); short linked paragraphs, the third picking up the second ('With powers set aside')

'Mutahhari's words show why seeking them would be: the goal has become...' — a garbled claim-colon-gloss compound; Author A writes two clean sentences ('Sheikh Bahmanpour calls such powers shirk. Mutahhari explains why seeking them would be so')
'One addresses the heart of the seeker, the other the eye of the one choosing a guide.' — balanced antithesis for effect; Author A states the point flatly
'Neither makes powers the aim of the path.' — tidy summary line closing the paragraph; Author A moves on to the next step instead
Whole passage is one long paragraph stacking two sources and three quotations; Author A gives each source its own short paragraph
'Murtada Mutahhari uses the lecturer's own word' — Author A never says 'the lecturer'; writes 'the same word as Sheikh Bahmanpour'
'The great teachers of the Shia tradition make closely related points, each in his own words.' — throat-clearing, grander opener; Author A opens on the specific scholar
'If even Paradise is not to be the goal, powers certainly are not.' — a tidy a-fortiori clincher at paragraph end; Author A avoids closing flourishes
Quotation after quotation chained with little spoken to them ('Whoever does so ... It is his own self that he worships, "though..."'); Author A gives one quotation and explains it

Quotation introduced by name, then explained in a plain sentence ('He cites them to show...'); next paragraph picks up ('Requests this high raise a difficulty'); comma-light 'and' joins as in the reference ('those brought near to God and he asks')

Short linking opener ('The third request is nearness and the Munajat makes it...'), quotation followed by a one-line gloss, and the 'For some of us... For others...' inclusive 'we/us' stance matches the reference

Plain reasoning in short sentences, 'Most of us...' contrast like 'Most of us see only the lamp', and each paragraph hands on to the next source ('Surah Fatir describes the same people by what they feel')

Mid-sentence 'he says' attributions and the chapter-close recap ('The Qur'an invites more than the minimum and what stands in the way is a faculty in us that can be repaired') echo the reference's argument and plain register, though the stacked 'he says' is heavier than usual

'These words come near the end of Duʿa Kumayl... The line asks God for...' mirrors the reference opening exactly in form; second paragraph links back to the previous chapter and states the chapter's job plainly
'The reward.' — a verbless signpost fragment; Author A never uses fragments, would write 'The first thing they receive is nearness'
'in the lecturer's reading' — Author A names him ('Sheikh Bahmanpour reads it as')
'It tells us what they receive and whether the rest of us can join them.' — sets up a teaser the passage does not answer; Author A states rather than withholds
'rise above the concerns that infect everyone else' — heightened, judgemental diction; Author A's register is plainer

Contrast stated plainly with a semicolon, then 'Sheikh Bahmanpour is careful about what this means' and a clear qualification; the next paragraph picks up with 'The Qur'an also tells us...' and a colon used for explanation as in the reference
Chapter recap in the reference's plain declarative style, with 'already on our lips' and 'more than the minimum' phrasing and a bare signpost to the Appendix rather than a flourish

Opens by picking up the last step ('If the receiver can be repaired...'), 'The word is khashiʿ and it means more than humble' matches the reference's gloss habit; the sentence-initial 'So' is the one slightly off note
